generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, progress often depends on how you handle a result that disappoints. A low mark on a physiology lab report can feel like a verdict on whether you belong in sport at all. A growth mindset reads it differently. It treats the mark as information about a specific skill, such as interpreting test data, that you can build with practice. Subjects across the school weigh that skill in their own way, through lab evidence, coaching judgement or clinical reasoning. All of them, though, reward the same response to a setback.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students get the same disappointing mark back on a physiology lab report they worked hard on.

Tom reads the mark, decides that lab work is just not something he is built for, and files the report away without opening the feedback. The effort felt wasted, so going back over it seems pointless. Nothing changes before the next practical. This is a fixed-mindset response: the mark is treated as a verdict on ability.

Amara is just as disappointed, but reads the feedback closely and notes two things that cost marks: a shaky interpretation of the VO2 max data and thin links to the underlying physiology. She turns these into two specific things to practise next time. The mark still stings, but it has become useful. This is a growth-mindset response: the mark is treated as information about what to do next.

Both students got the same mark. Only Amara let it move her learning forward.
generatedProse.summary: A growth mindset earns its place in the School of Sport when a result disappoints. A fixed response reads a poor mark as proof of your limits. A growth response reads it as information about a skill, such as interpreting test data or reading a session, that you can build. You can now tell the two responses apart, recognise a growth approach in action, and choose one yourself. The next lesson keeps you going once you have decided to carry on.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's approach a growth-mindset one?

items.text: She turned the feedback into specific things to practise, such as interpreting the VO2 max data more carefully.
She was less disappointed by the mark than Tom was.
She decided that lab work was simply not for her.
She filed the report away without opening the feedback.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara turned the feedback into specific things to practise, letting the mark move her learning forward.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID with the mark, beyond how she felt about it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara was growth-minded because she turned the feedback into specific things to practise. The other options describe the fixed response or just a feeling.
